toc.title: Pathway one: the brake turns off when you're triggered
Pathway two: the brake was never developed

blocks.p: Someone asked me: "Why is it that trauma survivors have a compromised vagal brake?" To answer that, we need to understand two things first: what the vagal brake is, and what we mean by trauma.
The vagal brake is the influence of your safety state on your heart. If those biological pathways, the ventral vagal pathways, are active, then your heartbeat stays at a calmer pace.

So the vagal brake is not a thing that lives inside of you. It's the influence of your safety state. If your safety state is active, it keeps the defensive states more at bay, which is to say that your heartbeat stays at a calmer pace.
Dr. Porges put it simply when he was on the podcast:

q: When you have an efficient vagal brake, if you take it off, your heart rate goes up. If you put it back on, it goes down.
blocks.cite: Stephen Porges, [Dr Stephen Porges: Polyvagal Theory Updates & Critiques (episode 201)](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/0e6ffc9f-a364-46e7-bb44-a17299f16de6)

blocks.p: When I talk about trauma, I'm talking about a stuck defensive autonomic nervous system. There are many different events, or lack of events, that can leave somebody in a traumatized state. But there are two basic pathways those events can take that lead to someone being stuck in a defensive state:

ol: Surviving a thing. You go through an acute traumatic incident that leaves you in a stuck defensive state. That could be a whole bunch of stuff, including all kinds of assaults, war, a car crash.

Repeated disconnection from safety. You make a connection, it gets cut off. You make a connection, it gets cut off. Your impulse to connect with safe others repeatedly gets cut off, and that also leaves you in a stuck defensive state. This is especially true in childhood, where you're probably more prone to this pathway.

blocks.p: Why the vagal brake is compromised depends on which pathway you went through.

blocks.h: Pathway one: the brake turns off when you're triggered

blocks.p: If you went through a thing, you could otherwise have pretty well developed safety pathways. Those ventral vagal pathways can develop, and then you go through a thing. Moment to moment, day to day, you may not be in a noticeable stuck defensive state, but that stuck defensive energy is still within you somewhere.

Then, when you're around the context of that thing, you get retriggered, and all of a sudden that stuck defensive energy surges. It might be stuck freeze energy, where you have flight or fight and shutdown at the same time, in that mixed state. When it surges during that trigger, your vagal brake is not strong enough. It's compromised. Basically, it turns off in that moment where you're triggered by a reminder of whatever you went through.

As a very stereotypical, basic example: a soldier goes to war and gets traumatized in an explosion. They come home, and they hear a loud sound. Their body is neurocepting danger. Their vagal brake comes off, meaning their safety system comes off, and now they're back in a flight or fight state. It surges within them. During that moment, their vagal brake is compromised. It's not on.

blocks.h: Pathway two: the brake was never developed

blocks.p: Someone who went through the second path, that repeated disconnection, simply does not develop those safety pathways to where they would be had they gotten good enough parenting. Not perfect parenting, but good enough parenting: enough to develop the safety pathways to live a functional life and make generally safe connections with people.

Without that, the safety pathways don't get developed enough. That means they don't have the capacity to recognize safety in others. They don't have the capacity to feel trust and vulnerability, or to have emotional regulation. Everything just kind of gets thrown off when we don't have good enough parenting.
So why is their vagal brake compromised? Because it was never developed. Their safety pathways simply are not strong enough.
The way I think about it, it's like exercising anything else in your body. If you want to be able to lift heavier stuff, you have to go through the reps to be able to lift heavier stuff.

Same thing if you want to be able to make safe connections with people, emotionally regulate, feel vulnerability, and identify safety. You have to have those safety pathways built up. You have to go through the reps to exercise them, so that they're strong enough to give you a vagal brake that can deal with the stuck defensive energy that might be inside of you.
So why do trauma survivors have a compromised vagal brake? It depends on which pathway you went through.
